questions.q: What single clause defines a tail-log backup, and where is it applied?
options: `WITH NORECOVERY`, applied to the `BACKUP LOG` statement itself
`WITH RECOVERY`, applied to the BACKUP LOG statement
`WITH REPLACE`, applied to the RESTORE DATABASE statement
`WITH STOPAT`, applied to the final RESTORE statement
questions.explain: A tail-log backup is an ordinary BACKUP LOG with WITH NORECOVERY added, which both captures the log and takes the database offline.

questions.q: What state does a database enter immediately after a tail-log backup completes?
options: READ_ONLY
SUSPECT
RESTORING — the same state produced by RESTORE ... WITH NORECOVERY
ONLINE, with no changes
questions.explain: The tail-log backup's WITH NORECOVERY takes the database out of action, leaving it in RESTORING state ready for a restore chain.

questions.q: When is a tail-log backup required, per this lesson?
options: Only when the recovery model is SIMPLE
Every single time any restore is performed, with no exceptions
Whenever the source database is still accessible and every transaction since the last log backup must be preserved before restoring
Only when restoring to a different server
questions.explain: A tail-log backup only makes sense — and is only possible — when the source database is still accessible to be backed up.

questions.q: Why is a tail-log backup impossible when the source database has suffered a total hardware failure?
options: A tail-log backup requires a working differential backup first
Hardware failures automatically convert the database to SIMPLE recovery
There's no accessible log left to back up — the transactions since the last log backup are genuinely unrecoverable
Tail-log backups are disabled after any hardware failure by SQL Server itself
questions.explain: If the drive holding the log is destroyed, there's nothing left to read the tail-log backup from — the restore chain simply ends at the last successful log backup.

questions.q: Why is skipping a tail-log backup on an accessible database especially risky during scripted restores?
options: Scripted restores always fail without a tail-log backup
Scripted restores automatically delete the transaction log
Tail-log backups are only possible through SSMS, never through T-SQL scripts
SSMS's restore wizard prompts for a tail-log backup automatically, but scripted restores get no such prompt, making it easy to forget under pressure
questions.explain: The built-in safety net exists in the SSMS GUI, not in raw T-SQL — so a DBA running scripted restores has to remember this step deliberately.
